ai-agent: The illustration shows a small apartment window at night, a person asleep with their laptop shut, while above the rooftops a glowing cloud contains a tidy computer workbench where a lead agent — a compact robot figure with a lanyard reading GOAL — sits at the center of a circular loop drawn in light: PLAN → ACT → OBSERVE → ADJUST, arrows chasing one another around. On its belt hang tool icons: a browser, a terminal window, a folder of files, and a code box; under the workbench, a miniature virtual machine hums with its own power light, showing the agent keeps working though the user's machine is off. Below the lead agent, three smaller specialist robots labor at their own tiny screens on tasks handed down by paper slips, none of them speaking to the sleeper directly — one monitors a feed, one fills a form, one assembles a document that grows page by page. But at one point on the loop, the act arrow wobbles and produces a red slip: a speech bubble escaping into a messaging app that should have only been searched, drifting out of place — while a translucent human hand, drawn in ghostly outline, rests on the workbench, having performed the task once while a camera icon recorded it, and a shield-shaped confirmation prompt stands ready near the loop's edge, one button green and waiting for a click.
ai-benchmark: A wide editorial illustration shows a group of diverse robot students sitting at identical desks in an examination hall, each working through the same printed test paper under the same harsh light — the essence of a benchmark as a shared exam. Along one wall, two grading stations make the entry's distinction visible: on the left, an automated machine stamps pages PASS or FAIL with mechanical arms (automatic scoring), while on the right, a human examiner with reading glasses thoughtfully assesses a real-world project, like a cluttered desk or a working machine (human judgment). At the center rear, a large glowing leaderboard board averages results into single ranked numbers for an audience of buyers holding shopping lists. But the scene carries deliberate warnings: one robot secretly glances at a crib sheet labeled "training data" peeking from under its desk, hinting that answers leaked into practice; a salesman by the door displays a cherry-picked chart showing only the flattering bar; and one robot with a top score sits helplessly tangled in an everyday task like tying a shoelace, showing scores don't guarantee real capability. In the foreground, a wise reviewer examines the leaderboard through a magnifying glass while also rolling up her sleeve to test a robot hands-on — capturing the entry's final point: benchmarks are evidence to be weighed, not verdicts.
frontier-model: A wide, tilted mountain ridge shaped like a jagged line graph rises across the composition, its shifting summit never settled: three or four small flags planted by rival expedition camps crowd the peak, each camp tugging a rope that briefly hoists its own flag above the others before another camp's climbers overtake it, while older, faded flags litter the slopes below to show that leadership constantly changes hands. The mountain itself dissolves at the top into a hazy, unmeasured region with no marked summit or official boundary line — the last surveyor's marker sits well below where the camps actually stand, and a banner of question marks drifts where a defined threshold should be. Around the base, an entire economy gravitates upward: coins, price tags, and arrows of investment flow toward whoever currently holds the peak, and silhouetted engineers climb toward the camps. In the foreground, two figures assess the mountain differently — one studies an official leaderboard scroll with ranked bars, the other tests a rope by hand, and each figure's judgment disagrees with the other's, one scroll showing a camp near the top that the hands-on tester finds flimsy, while a humbler camp she has tested proves surprisingly solid.
post-training: A single wide cross-section illustration that reads left to right like an assembly line of learning. On the far left stands an enormous, dark pretraining hall: entire rivers of books are shredded into a conveyor-belt stream of single words, while a huge, blank, grey robot must call out each next word before it lands; a giant fuel gauge on the hall's wall shows nearly all the computing fuel being spent here. The grey robot then walks into a much smaller, sunlit post-training school occupying the rest of the scene. First a classroom, where the robot drills through stacks of neatly worked exam solutions projected on a chalkboard; a gauge on its chest labelled "knowledge" stays frozen at the same level, while a grinding wheel beside it visibly sharpens a blade labelled "skill." Next a gymnasium, where examiners hold up scorecards stamped "pass/fail" and "thumbs up/down," and the robot repeats one answer over and over, bending toward the answers marked correct and preferred. At the exit stand two robots cast from the very same mold, joined by a tag reading "same base model": one clumsy and fumbling, the other poised and useful. In the foreground, the older grey robot writes pages that drop into a basket; a human editor discards some and feeds the rest into a brand-new textbook lying open before a small young robot waiting to begin.
tokens-and-pricing: The illustration depicts two AI models at workstations, each receiving the same small task card from a conveyor belt of rectangular tiles, where every tile carries just a few letters of a word, showing that text is chopped into tiny metered chunks called tokens. Beside each model stands a taximeter-style gauge posting the going rate, with incoming token tiles priced low and outgoing tiles several times higher, tallied per million, because writing text costs more computation than reading it. The model advertised as cheap sprays an enormous cascade of tiles, most of them drifting semi-transparently through a thought bubble labeled private reasoning before reaching a short final answer, so its bill runs high; next to it, the expensive model emits only a brief, tidy answer with a tiny thought bubble, and its bill comes out lower, while a banner over both stations reads price times how much it writes equals cost per task. In the foreground, a consumer chat app keeps its meter hidden behind a flat monthly price tag, while a developer beside it studies an invoice itemizing millions of tokens in and out, the whole arithmetic laid bare on paper.
